messages.content: What is the true purpose of the human heart?
The heart is a muscular pump that drives blood through the arteries and veins, carrying oxygen and nourishment to every part of the body.
Why does the body have a liver at all?
The liver filters impurities from the blood, produces bile to aid digestion, and stores nourishment for later use by the body.
What actually causes a fever?
A fever is the body's natural response to infection, in which the internal temperature rises to help fight off harmful germs.
Why does the brain feel cool when touched during dissection?
The brain is the seat of the nervous system, governing thought, sensation, and the working of the whole body.
What function does the spleen serve in the body?
The spleen filters the blood, removes worn-out red corpuscles, and assists the body in fighting infection.
Why do people sneeze?
A sneeze is a reflex that expels dust, pollen, or other irritants from the nasal passages.
Why does the skin rise into goosebumps in the cold?
Tiny muscles at the base of each hair contract, a leftover reflex from ancestors whose fur once trapped warmth.
What are the kidneys for?
The kidneys filter waste products and excess water from the blood, forming the urine that the body expels.
Why do the eyes water when a person weeps?
Emotion prompts the tear glands to produce fluid, which also serves ordinarily to keep the eyes moist and clean.
What brings on an attack of hiccups?
Hiccups are caused by a sudden, involuntary spasm of the diaphragm, the muscle beneath the lungs.
Why do people yawn when weary?
A yawn is thought to help draw fresh air into the lungs and rouse the brain, and it is well known to be contagious among companions.
What is the appendix for?
The appendix is a small pouch near the start of the large intestine, believed to play some part in the body's immune defences.
Why does a person's hair turn gray with age?
Hair turns gray because the cells that give it colour gradually produce less pigment as a person grows older.
What is the true office of the nerves in the body?
The nerves carry signals, both electrical and chemical, between the brain and every part of the body, governing sensation and movement.
Why do fingernails keep growing throughout life?
Cells at the base of the nail, called the matrix, continually produce new tissue, pushing the nail forward as it grows.
What determines whether a man's disposition is gentle or fierce?
A person's disposition arises from upbringing, temperament, and the workings of the brain, not from the shape of the skull.
Why does the stomach make a growling noise when a person is hungry?
The growling is caused by the muscular walls of the empty stomach and intestine contracting and moving air and fluid along.
What purpose does the pancreas serve?
The pancreas produces juices that aid digestion and also makes insulin, which governs the sugar carried in the blood.
Why does a person's face redden when embarrassed?
Blushing occurs when nerves widen the small blood vessels of the face in response to strong feeling, letting more blood show through the skin.
What is the true purpose of the lungs?
The lungs take in oxygen from the air and pass it to the blood, while removing carbon dioxide that the body no longer needs.
Why does thunder follow lightning rather than come at the same instant?
Light travels far faster than sound, so we see the flash almost at once but hear the thunder only after the sound has journeyed to us across the intervening air.
What causes the wind to blow?
Wind arises from differences in air pressure between regions, the air moving from areas of high pressure toward areas of low pressure to even things out.
Why do we see a rainbow after a rain shower?
Sunlight passing through raindrops is bent and separated into its component colours, which appear to us arranged in a coloured arc in the sky.
What makes hail form during a storm?
Hail forms when strong updrafts carry raindrops repeatedly through freezing layers of the cloud, adding layers of ice until the stones grow too heavy to be held aloft.
Why does the sky sometimes turn greenish before a severe storm?
The greenish cast comes from sunlight passing through a great depth of water droplets and ice in a large, thick storm cloud, which filters the light in that peculiar way.
What causes a tornado to form?
A tornado forms when a rotating column of air within a thunderstorm, driven by shifting winds of differing speed and direction, is drawn down toward the ground by the storm's updraft.
Why is it colder at the top of a mountain than in the valley below, even though it is nearer the sun?
As air rises it expands and cools, so that mountain air, being less dense and having expanded, holds less heat than the denser air of the valley.
What causes fog to form on a still morning?
Fog forms when moist air near the ground cools during the night until its water vapour condenses into tiny droplets suspended in the air.
Why do storms tend to be worse at sea than on land?
Storms often intensify over open water because the sea supplies abundant moisture and heat to the air, feeding the storm's energy with fewer obstacles to slow its winds.
What makes snowflakes always have six sides?
The six-sided form arises from the way water molecules bond together as they freeze, which naturally produces a hexagonal crystal lattice.
Why does a storm often bring a sudden drop in temperature?
A storm often ushers in a mass of cooler air from another region, and the arrival of this air, along with rain evaporating and drawing heat from its surroundings, brings the temperature down.
What causes the different shapes of clouds we see in the sky?
Cloud shapes depend upon the height, temperature, and movement of the air in which they form, with rising currents producing towering clouds and stable air producing flat, layered ones.
Why does lightning strike tall objects such as trees and towers?
Tall objects offer the shortest path for the electrical charge between cloud and ground, so lightning is more likely to strike them than the lower ground around them.
What makes the wind change direction before a storm arrives?
As a storm system approaches, the arrangement of high and low pressure areas around it shifts, causing the wind to swing round to match the changing pattern.
Why do we sometimes see our breath as mist on a cold day?
The warm, moist air we exhale meets the cold outside air and its water vapour condenses into tiny droplets, which appear to us as a visible mist.
What causes a halo to appear around the sun or moon on certain days?
A halo appears when light from the sun or moon is bent as it passes through ice crystals high in the atmosphere, forming a ring around the light source.
Why does thunder sometimes rumble on for a long while instead of ending in a single crack?
The rumbling occurs because the sound travels to us from different points along the long path of the lightning bolt, each part arriving at a slightly different time.
What makes a barometer useful for predicting a storm?
A barometer measures air pressure, and since falling pressure often signals an approaching storm, watching the barometer's movement helps foretell changes in the weather.
Why is the air often very still just before a severe thunderstorm breaks?
The calm often occurs because the warm, humid air near the ground is being drawn upward into the building storm, leaving the surface air undisturbed until the storm's front arrives.
What causes the roaring sound heard from a distant hurricane or great storm?
The roar comes from the combined noise of powerful winds, crashing waves, and turbulent air moving over a wide area, blending into one continuous sound as it reaches distant ears.
Why do the stars twinkle at night?
Stars twinkle because their light is bent this way and that by moving currents of air in our own atmosphere, not by any change in the stars themselves.
What causes the phases of the Moon?
The Moon's phases arise because we see varying portions of its sunlit half as it circles the Earth, the Sun always lighting one side of it.
Why does Mars appear reddish in the sky?
Mars appears reddish because its surface is rich in iron oxide, the same rust-colored mineral found in certain earthly soils.
What are shooting stars?
Shooting stars are small bits of rock or dust burning up from friction as they plunge through our atmosphere at great speed.
Why do we always see the same face of the Moon?
We see only one face of the Moon because it rotates once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit the Earth once.
What makes the Sun so hot?
The Sun's heat arises from nuclear processes deep within it, where lighter elements are fused into heavier ones, releasing tremendous energy.
Why does the sky turn dark at night instead of staying bright with starlight?
Night is dark chiefly because the stars, though numerous, are so distant and faint that their combined light cannot rival the day.
What are the rings of Saturn made of?
Saturn's rings are composed of countless small particles of ice and rock, orbiting the planet in a thin, flat disk.
Why do planets move differently across the sky than stars?
Planets appear to wander because they orbit the Sun at varying speeds and distances, unlike the fixed stars, which lie far beyond our system.
What causes a solar eclipse?
A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Earth and the Sun, casting its shadow upon us.
Why is Venus so bright in the evening sky?
Venus is bright because it is covered in thick, reflective clouds and lies relatively close to both the Sun and the Earth.
What are comets, and why do they have tails?
Comets are icy bodies that develop long tails of gas and dust when solar heat causes their frozen material to vaporize as they near the Sun.
Why does the Moon sometimes appear larger near the horizon?
The Moon appears larger near the horizon due to an optical illusion of the eye and mind; its actual size and distance remain unchanged.
What holds the planets in their orbits around the Sun?
The planets are held in orbit by the Sun's gravitational pull, which balances against their forward motion through space.
Why does Jupiter have such a great number of moons?
Jupiter has many moons because its immense mass exerts a strong gravitational pull, capable of holding numerous smaller bodies in orbit.
What is the Milky Way that stretches across the night sky?
The Milky Way is the combined light of countless stars in our own galaxy, seen edge-on from our position within it.
Why do the stars seem to move across the sky through the night?
The stars appear to move because the Earth itself rotates on its axis, carrying us beneath the fixed pattern of the heavens.
What causes the seasons to change throughout the year?
The seasons change because the Earth's axis is tilted, so different parts of the globe receive more or less direct sunlight through the year.
Why does the Moon have craters upon its surface?
The Moon's craters were formed chiefly by the impact of meteorites over countless ages, its surface lacking air or water to wear them smooth.
What is the North Star, and why does it not seem to move?
The North Star, Polaris, lies nearly in line with the Earth's axis of rotation, so it appears to remain almost stationary while other stars wheel about it.
Why do bears sleep through the whole winter?
Bears hibernate because their bodily processes slow to conserve the fat reserves built up in autumn, allowing them to survive the lean winter months without feeding.
How do bats manage to fly about so surely in the dark?
Bats emit high-pitched sounds beyond our hearing and judge their surroundings by the echoes that return to them, a faculty we call echolocation.
Why do dogs howl when the moon is full?
Dogs howl to communicate across distance, an inherited habit from their wolf ancestors, and the practice has no true connection to the moon itself.
What makes a cat purr when it is content?
Purring is produced by rapid vibration of the muscles about the cat's larynx, and it commonly accompanies contentment, though sometimes distress as well.
Where do the swallows go when winter comes?
Swallows migrate great distances to warmer countries, returning again when the weather turns mild in their native land.
How does the chameleon change its colour so readily?
The chameleon possesses special cells in its skin that expand or contract in response to light, temperature, and mood, thereby altering its colour.
Why do salmon fight their way upstream to spawn?
Salmon return by scent and instinct to the very stream where they were hatched, there to lay their eggs in familiar waters.
What makes a spider able to spin its web?
The spider possesses glands that produce liquid silk, which hardens upon contact with air as it is drawn out to form the web.
How is it that owls can see so well after dark?
The owl's eyes are large with pupils that open wide, and its retina holds many cells especially sensitive to dim light.
Why does a snake shed its skin from time to time?
A snake's skin does not grow as the animal grows, and so it must periodically shed the old skin to make way for a larger one beneath.
How do bees turn flower nectar into honey?
Bees gather nectar and mix it with enzymes in their bodies, then store it in the comb where much of its water evaporates, leaving thick honey.
Why does the peacock spread its splendid tail?
The peacock spreads its tail as a courtship display, to attract a mate by the brilliance of its plumage.
Why are moths so drawn to a lit lamp at night?
Moths ordinarily steer by the moon and stars, and a bright artificial light disturbs this natural guidance, drawing them off their course.
What causes the cricket's chirping on a summer night?
The male cricket produces its chirp by rubbing specialised parts of its wings together, chiefly to attract a mate.
Why does the hedgehog roll itself into a tight ball?
The hedgehog rolls into a ball to present its sharp spines outward on every side, a defence against any creature that would trouble it.
Why does the squirrel bury nuts about the wood?
The squirrel buries nuts to provide itself with food through the winter, and finds them again chiefly by memory and by scent.
Why does a whale send up a spout of water from its head?
The whale exhales warm breath through its blowhole, and this breath, meeting the cool air, condenses into the visible spout we observe.
Why do frogs set up such a croaking after dark?
The male frog croaks to attract a mate, the sound greatly amplified by a vocal sac that swells beneath its throat.
Why has the elephant so long and useful a trunk?
The elephant's trunk is a fusion of nose and upper lip, grown long and muscular, and serves the animal for breathing, smelling, and grasping alike.
How does the octopus alter its colour so swiftly?
The octopus possesses special pigment cells called chromatophores, governed by its nerves, which it can expand or contract to change colour for camouflage.
Why do the leaves of plants turn green?
Leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll, a substance that captures sunlight and converts it, with water and air, into the plant's food.
Why do the leaves fall from the trees each autumn?
As days shorten, chlorophyll breaks down and a layer of cells forms at each leaf's base, so it loosens and falls.
Why does a plant on the windowsill lean toward the light?
This bending, called phototropism, occurs because a growth substance in the stem gathers on the shaded side, making it elongate faster there.
What is it that makes certain flowers so sweetly scented?
The scent comes from volatile oils in the petals, which serve chiefly to attract bees and other insects for pollination.
Why does a seed left in damp earth begin to sprout?
The seed absorbs water, which awakens enzymes that convert its stored starch into food for the growing embryo.
Why does the grass seem greener after a rain?
Rain supplies water and dissolved nitrogen the grass needs, and growth that had slowed for want of moisture resumes at once.
How is it that mushrooms appear in a field overnight?
A network of fungal threads already lies hidden in the soil, and it sends up its fruiting bodies with remarkable speed once the air is moist.
Why are some fruits sour while others of the same tree are sweet?
The proportion of sugar to acid varies with the fruit's ripeness and its particular variety.
Why does a tree trunk show rings when it is cut?
Each ring represents one year's growth, wider in years of good rainfall and narrower in lean, dry ones.
Why do climbing vines wind themselves about a pole?
The tendril is sensitive to touch, and contact with the pole stimulates one side to grow faster than the other, causing it to curl round.
Why does the cutting of an onion bring tears to the eyes?
Cutting releases sulfur compounds that react with the moisture on the eye's surface, forming a mild irritant that provokes tears.
Why does ivy cling so firmly to a stone wall?
Ivy puts out small rootlets along its stem that secrete a sticky substance, gripping tightly to any rough surface.
Why do certain plants fold their leaves together at nightfall?
This folding, called nyctinasty, is governed by the plant's own daily rhythm, which alters the pressure of fluid within the leaf's cells.
Why does a plant wilt so quickly in the summer heat?
In great heat the plant loses water through its leaves faster than the roots can replace it, so the cells lose their firmness and it droops.
Why does the carrot's root grow down into the earth while its leaves reach up toward the sky?
Both root and shoot respond to gravity, but in opposite ways -- the root growing downward and the shoot upward, a response called gravitropism.
Why does a potato left in a dark cellar begin to sprout eyes?
The potato's dormant buds, called eyes, begin to grow once warmth and moisture are sufficient, with or without light.
Why does one apple tree bear abundant fruit while its neighbor bears none at all?
Fruiting depends on proper pollination and the tree's maturity; a young tree, or one lacking a suitable pollinator nearby, will bear little or none.
Why is moss so often found only on the north side of a tree trunk?
The north side of the trunk stays shaded and damp longer through the day, and moss thrives best where moisture lingers.
Why must a plant have sunlight in order to grow at all?
The plant uses the energy of sunlight, in a process called photosynthesis, to convert water and air into the sugars that nourish it.
Why do rose bushes grow sharp thorns along their stems?
Thorns are a modified growth of the stem that help discourage grazing animals from eating the plant.
Why does a poker glow red when thrust into the fire?
The poker glows because its atoms are agitated to great speed by the heat, and this agitation radiates energy as visible light.
What causes the shimmering haze above a hot road on a summer day?
It is caused by layers of air at different temperatures bending light unevenly, an effect called a mirage.
Why does a candle flame point upward rather than sideways?
The hot gases produced by burning are lighter than the surrounding cool air and rise, drawing the flame upward with them.
Why do some coals glow after the flame has died away?
The coal continues to combust slowly, and its surface remains hot enough to emit visible light even without an open flame.
Why does ice feel cold to the touch?
Ice draws heat rapidly from the warmer hand, and the sensation of cold is simply the loss of that heat being felt by the skin.
What makes the sky bright with light even when the sun itself cannot be seen?
Sunlight is scattered in all directions by the molecules of the atmosphere, which brightens the whole sky even on a cloudy day.
Why does rubbing two sticks together eventually produce fire?
Friction converts the effort of rubbing into heat, and enough heat gathered in one spot will ignite the wood's fibers.
Why does a mirror reflect light so clearly compared to a plain wall?
The smooth, polished surface of the mirror reflects light rays at equal and opposite angles, preserving their original order and forming a clear image.
Why does the north side of a house feel cooler than the south side in winter?
The south side receives more direct sunlight through the day, warming it more than the shaded north side.
Why does a lit match go out when plunged into water?
Water absorbs heat from the flame faster than the match can produce it, cooling the burning material below its ignition point.
Why does the moon shine at night?
The moon has no light of its own; it merely reflects sunlight from its surface toward the earth.
Why does a flame burn blue at its base and yellow higher up?
The blue region is where combustion is most complete and hottest, while the yellow above comes from unburnt carbon particles glowing as they rise.
Why do we see our breath as a small cloud on a cold morning?
The warm, moist air from our lungs cools rapidly outside the body, causing the water vapor within it to condense into tiny visible droplets.
Why does metal feel hotter than wood when both sit in the same sunny room?
Metal conducts heat much faster than wood, so it transfers warmth into your hand more quickly, making it feel hotter.
Why does a rainbow appear after a rain shower?
Sunlight is refracted and separated into its component colours as it passes through raindrops, forming the familiar arc.
Why does a stove make the whole room warm rather than just the air right beside it?
Heat spreads through the room by convection currents of warmed air and by radiation from the stove's hot surface.
Why does staring at the sun hurt the eyes?
The sun's intense light overwhelms and can damage the delicate cells of the retina at the back of the eye.
Why does a glass of water left in sunlight grow slightly warm?
The water absorbs energy from the sunlight passing through and around it, and this absorbed energy raises its temperature.
Why do sparks fly upward from a bonfire?
Sparks are tiny burning particles carried upward by the strong rising current of hot air above the fire.
Why does the flame of a lamp burn steadily in still air but flicker in a draught?
Moving air disturbs the steady supply of oxygen and the rising column of hot gas, causing the flame to bend and flicker.
Why does ice float upon water instead of sinking?
Ice floats because water expands as it freezes, making ice less dense than the liquid water beneath it.
Why is the sea salty while rivers taste fresh?
Rivers dissolve minerals from rocks and soil as they flow, and carry these salts to the sea, where the water evaporates but the salt remains, gradually concentrating over ages.
What causes the tides to rise and fall each day?
The tides are caused chiefly by the gravitational pull of the moon, and to a lesser extent the sun, upon the earth's oceans.
Why does water become invisible steam when it boils?
Boiling gives water molecules enough heat energy to escape into the air as vapour, which is invisible until it cools and condenses into visible mist.
Why do icebergs appear blue in certain light?
Icebergs appear blue because dense glacial ice absorbs red light and scatters the remaining blue light, much as the sky does.
Why does a pond freeze first at its surface rather than throughout?
Cold air chills the surface water first, and since ice is less dense than water, it forms and remains at the top while warmer water sinks below.
Why does seawater not freeze as readily as fresh water?
Dissolved salt lowers the freezing point of water, so seawater must be chilled considerably colder than fresh water before ice will form.
What causes waves to form upon the surface of the sea?
Waves are chiefly caused by wind blowing across the water's surface, transferring its energy and pushing the water into moving crests and troughs.
Why does a ship of iron float upon the water?
A ship floats because its hollow shape displaces a volume of water whose weight equals the ship's own weight, providing sufficient buoyant support.
Why does fog form over the sea on certain mornings?
Sea fog forms when warm, moist air passes over cooler water, causing the water vapour in the air to condense into tiny visible droplets.
Why does dew appear upon grass near the water's edge in the morning?
Dew forms when the night air cools, causing water vapour in the air to condense upon the cool surfaces of grass and leaves.
Why do whirlpools sometimes form in rivers and seas?
Whirlpools form where opposing currents, tides, or the shape of the seabed cause water to circulate rapidly around a central point.
Why does the sea appear a different colour in different places?
The sea's colour depends chiefly on the way sunlight is scattered and absorbed by the water, along with suspended particles, depth, and the reflection of the sky.
Why does ice feel colder to the touch than water at the same temperature?
Ice conducts heat away from the skin more efficiently than liquid water does, and it is generally colder to begin with, since it must be at or below freezing.
Why do bubbles rise when water is heated in a pot?
As water is heated, dissolved air is driven out and, at boiling, water itself turns to vapour, both forming bubbles that rise because they are lighter than the surrounding liquid.
Why does a stone thrown into a pond cause ripples that spread outward in circles?
The stone's impact disturbs the water, and this disturbance travels outward evenly in all directions as a wave, forming expanding circles.
Why is it harder to float in a swimming pool than in the sea?
Salt dissolved in seawater increases its density, so the sea provides greater buoyancy than the less dense fresh water typically found in a swimming pool.
Why does the surface of still water form a thin skin that can support a floating needle?
Water molecules attract one another strongly at the surface, creating a thin elastic film called surface tension, which can support small light objects.
Why do icebergs calve, breaking away from glaciers, in the warmer months?
As temperatures rise, glacier ice melts and weakens at its edges, and the constant stress of gravity and moving ice eventually causes large sections to break off into the sea.
Why does hot water sometimes appear to steam more than cold water when poured outdoors on a chilly day?
Hot water evaporates more readily, and when this warm vapour meets the cold air, it condenses quickly into a visible mist.
Why does gold never rust or tarnish, no matter how old it is?
Gold is a noble metal, chemically inert under ordinary conditions, and so it resists oxidation almost entirely.
What is it that makes a diamond harder than any other stone?
A diamond is pure carbon whose atoms are locked into a tight, rigid lattice, which gives it its extraordinary hardness.
Why does an iron tool left out in the wet grow rusty?
Iron combines slowly with oxygen and moisture in the air to form iron oxide, which we call rust.
What gives a lodestone its power to draw iron to itself?
A lodestone's tiny magnetic domains are aligned in one direction, producing a magnetic field that attracts iron.
How does coal come to be buried so deep in the earth?
Coal forms from ancient plant matter buried and slowly compressed under heat and pressure over vast ages.
Why is mercury a liquid metal when all the others are solid?
Mercury's atoms bond weakly to one another, giving it an unusually low melting point that keeps it liquid at room temperature.
Why does a copper roof turn green after years of weather?
Copper reacts slowly with air and moisture to form a green patina of copper carbonate on its surface.
How can a stone like pumice float upon water?
Pumice is riddled with tiny trapped gas bubbles from its volcanic origin, which make it far less dense than water.
What is the cause of the deep red color in a ruby?
A ruby is corundum colored red by traces of chromium locked within its crystal structure.
How do the hanging stone icicles in a cave come to form?
Mineral-laden water slowly dissolves limestone and redeposits it, building stalactites and stalagmites over centuries.
Why does flint throw off a spark when struck with steel?
The blow shaves off tiny fragments of hot metal, which glow and ignite briefly upon meeting the air.
Why does silver go black and tarnished if left too long unpolished?
Silver reacts with sulfur compounds present in the air, forming a dark coating of silver sulfide.
Why is a bar of lead so much heavier than a bar of iron the same size?
Lead atoms are simply heavier and more tightly packed than iron atoms, giving the metal greater density.
How can graphite and diamond be so different when both are carbon?
The two differ only in how their carbon atoms are arranged, graphite in loose sheets and diamond in a rigid lattice.
Why does burning sulfur give off such a foul odor?
Burning sulfur combines with oxygen to form sulfur dioxide, a gas with a sharp, unpleasant smell.
What is responsible for the green color found in emeralds?
An emerald is beryl colored green by small traces of chromium or vanadium within its crystal.
Why does asbestos cloth fail to catch fire like ordinary fabric?
Asbestos is a mineral fiber with a structure that will not combust, unlike fibers of plant or animal origin.
What truly separates granite from marble as building stones?
Granite is an igneous rock formed from cooling magma, while marble is limestone that has been recrystallized by heat and pressure.
Why is fine quartz crystal so clear while other stones are cloudy?
Pure quartz is silicon dioxide arranged in an orderly lattice with very few impurities, which keeps it transparent.
How do the hollow crystal-lined geodes found in the ground come to be?
A geode forms when mineral-rich water slowly deposits crystals along the walls of a hollow cavity within rock.
Why does thunder rumble on after we have already seen the lightning flash?
Light travels far faster than sound, so the flash reaches the eye almost at once while the sound takes longer to arrive, and echoes off clouds and hills draw out the rumble.
Why can I hear a train whistle before I can see the train coming round the bend?
Sound waves bend around obstacles such as a hillside or wall, a property called diffraction, while our sight is blocked by the bend itself.
Why does my own voice sound so different when I hear it played back from a phonograph record?
Ordinarily we hear our voice partly through vibrations carried by the bones of our own skull, and a recording lacks that inner conduction, so it sounds thinner and unfamiliar.
Why do large bells sound so much deeper than small ones?
A larger, heavier bell vibrates more slowly than a small one, and slower vibrations are heard by us as a lower note.
Why can sound be heard clearly even underwater?
Water is denser and more elastic than air, so it carries vibrations efficiently, and in fact sound travels through it even faster than through air.
Why does plucking a violin string make a musical note?
The plucked string vibrates rapidly to and fro at a steady rate, and this regular vibration of the air is what our ear perceives as a musical tone.
Why do some people have deep voices and others high, piping ones?
Pitch of voice depends chiefly on the length and thickness of the vocal cords; longer, thicker cords vibrate more slowly and so produce a deeper voice.
Why does holding a seashell to the ear seem to bring the roar of the ocean?
The shell's hollow, curved shape gathers and amplifies the faint sounds always present in the air about us, and these are heard as a steady roar resembling surf.
Why does shouting into a canyon send back an echo of our own words?
An echo happens when sound waves strike a hard, distant surface and bounce back to the ear after the brief interval needed to travel there and back.
Why do soldiers marching in step sometimes set a bridge swaying beneath them?
When the marching rhythm happens to match the bridge's own natural rate of vibration, resonance occurs and the small swayings build upon one another.
Why does a tuning fork always give the very same note no matter how it is struck?
The fork's fixed size and shape determine its natural rate of vibration, so it always sounds the same pitch, though a harder strike makes it louder, not higher.
Why is there no sound to be heard out among the stars?
Sound requires some material substance, such as air, to travel through, and since the space beyond our atmosphere is nearly empty of matter, no sound can pass through it.
Why does music sound higher in pitch when a phonograph record is spun too quickly?
Spinning the record faster increases the rate of the vibrations it reproduces, and a faster vibration is heard by the ear as a higher pitch.
Why does a bare, empty room make voices sound loud and booming?
Hard, bare walls reflect sound waves instead of absorbing them, so echoes and resonance accumulate and make the voice seem far louder than it truly is.
Why can a whisper spoken beneath a great dome be heard clearly by someone standing far across the hall?
The curved surface of the dome reflects the sound waves along its inner face, focusing them so that a whisper travels clearly to a distant point.
Why do longer organ pipes produce lower notes than shorter ones?
The length of the column of air inside the pipe fixes the rate at which it vibrates, and a longer column vibrates more slowly, giving a lower note.
Why does tapping a wine glass with a spoon make it ring out with a clear tone?
The tap sets the glass vibrating at its own natural frequency, and it is these vibrations of the glass that we hear as a ringing tone.
Why can a singer's voice sometimes shatter a wine glass by holding a certain note?
If the singer's note matches the glass's own natural frequency, the vibrations build upon one another through resonance until the glass can no longer bear them and breaks.
Why does a train whistle or church bell seem to carry farther and clearer on a still night?
At night the air near the ground is cooler than the air above, and this bends the sound waves back down toward the earth instead of letting them escape upward, so sound carries farther.
Why do a violin and a trumpet sound so different even when playing the very same note?
Each instrument produces its own particular blend of fainter overtones along with the main note, and this blend, called timbre, gives every instrument its distinctive character of sound.
What exactly is electricity that runs along the telegraph wire?
Electricity is the flow of electric charge, carried by electrons moving through the conducting wire, driven onward by the difference in potential supplied by the battery.
How does a telegraph send words across hundreds of miles almost instantly?
The operator opens and closes an electric circuit in patterns known as Morse code, and the resulting pulses of current travel along the wire to be read at the receiving end.
Why must a telegraph wire be insulated?
Insulation keeps the current from leaking away to the ground or to neighboring wires, so that it is confined to travel along the intended conductor.
What causes a lightning bolt during a thunderstorm?
Lightning is a great electrical discharge that leaps between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground, once opposite charges have built up sufficiently.
Why do I sometimes feel a small shock upon touching a metal doorknob?
The shock comes from static electricity that built up on your body as you moved across a carpet or other surface, discharging suddenly to the metal.
How does a battery produce its electric current?
A battery produces current through a chemical reaction between its metal plates and the acid within, which frees electrons to flow through the connected circuit.
What allows a telegraph signal to travel beneath the ocean through a submarine cable?
The cable holds an insulated copper conductor that carries the electric current directly through the depths, the surrounding gutta-percha keeping the signal from leaking into the sea.
Why does an electromagnet attract iron only when the current is switched on?
The flowing current generates a magnetic field only while it moves through the coil, and it is this field which magnetizes the iron core temporarily.
What makes an electric light bulb glow?
The bulb glows because the current heats a slender filament inside it until the filament becomes white hot and gives off light.
How does a telegraph operator distinguish one letter from another in the code?
Each letter is rendered as a distinct pattern of short and long pulses, dots and dashes, which the operator learns to read by the rhythm of the clicking sounder.
Why does copper wire carry electricity better than, say, a length of wood?
Copper conducts well because its atoms readily release electrons that move freely through the metal, while wood's structure hinders any such free movement.
What purpose does the ground wire serve in a telegraph line?
The ground wire completes the electrical circuit by returning the current to the earth, which serves as a common conductor, so that a single overhead wire may suffice.
Why are telegraph wires strung high upon poles above the road?
The wires are raised upon poles to keep them clear of people, animals, and passing traffic, and to prevent them from touching the earth or other obstacles.
What happens inside a telegraph key the instant the operator presses it down?
Pressing the key closes an electrical contact, completing the circuit so that current flows onward to the receiving station for as long as it remains depressed.
Why does touching the two ends of a live wire together sometimes make a spark?
The spark occurs because the current arcs briefly across the small gap of air as the conductors are joined or parted, momentarily setting the air aglow.
What is the static electricity one notices when combing dry hair?
It is caused by the transfer of electrons between the comb and the hair, leaving one with an excess of charge and the other a deficiency.
How does a telegraph relay carry a message over very long distances?
A relay uses a weak incoming current to trip a fresh local battery circuit, renewing the signal's strength so that it may continue on to the next station.
Why does an electric current heat a wire, as in a stove element?
The current heats the wire because the metal resists the flow of electrons, and this resistance converts a portion of the electrical energy into heat.
What is the difference between direct current and alternating current?
Direct current flows steadily in a single direction, while alternating current reverses its direction periodically, as produced by a generator whose coil turns within a magnetic field.
How does a dynamo generate electricity from mechanical motion?
A dynamo generates electricity by rotating a coil of wire within a magnetic field, which induces a current in the wire by the principle of electromagnetic induction.
Why do some men have a natural talent for music?
It is owing to an innate aptitude of ear and coordination, refined and strengthened through early exposure and diligent practice.
What makes a person courageous in the face of danger?
Courage arises from temperament and training together, whereby a person learns through experience and will to master the instinct of fear.
Why do some children learn to read more quickly than others?
It is owing to differences in native aptitude, early practice, and the quality of teaching and encouragement they receive.
What causes a melancholy disposition?
A melancholy disposition arises from a combination of inherited temperament and life circumstance, and may often be eased by occupation, exercise, and companionship.
Why do some people have quick tempers?
A quick temper generally reflects an inherited disposition together with habits of self-control that may be strengthened or neglected through upbringing.
How can one tell a person's character by looking at their face?
One cannot reliably judge character from the face alone; expression and conduct over time are far surer guides than any feature of countenance.
Why does a person sometimes lose their memory in old age?
Memory often declines in old age owing to gradual changes in the brain's tissue and circulation, though the rate varies greatly from person to person.
What makes a person clever with numbers?
A talent for numbers arises from natural aptitude combined with practice, much as any other skill is cultivated through repeated exercise.
Why do twins sometimes have very different personalities?
Even twins develop distinct personalities because experience, upbringing, and countless small differences in circumstance shape character alongside inherited traits.
What causes stubbornness in a person's nature?
Stubbornness reflects a strong-willed temperament, often shaped by upbringing and by a person's confidence in their own judgment.
Why do some people dream more vividly than others?
Vivid dreaming varies from person to person and seems tied to the depth and stage of sleep, as well as to individual imagination and recent experience.
What makes a person naturally cheerful?
A cheerful nature arises from inherited temperament together with favorable circumstances, good health, and habits of optimism.
Why do some people have a gift for persuading others?
A gift for persuasion generally comes from social intelligence, confidence, and practiced skill in reading and addressing an audience.
What causes a child to be shy among strangers?
Shyness generally reflects a cautious temperament, often shaped by upbringing and by limited experience with unfamiliar company.
Why do some people remember faces better than names?
Faces are recognized through visual memory, which for most people is more immediate and vivid than the verbal memory required to recall names.
What makes a person prone to jealousy?
Jealousy generally arises from insecurity and fear of loss, often shaped by past experience and by one's sense of one's own worth.
Why can some people concentrate for hours while others cannot?
Sustained concentration depends upon temperament, practice, interest in the task, and freedom from fatigue or distraction.
What causes a person to be naturally suspicious of others?
A suspicious nature often arises from past disappointment or betrayal, combined with an inherited caution of temperament.
Why do some people have vivid imaginations while others are more literal-minded?
A vivid imagination arises from natural inclination and habit of mind, often nurtured by exposure to stories, art, and creative pursuits.
What makes some people natural leaders?
Natural leadership arises from a combination of confidence, judgment, and the ability to inspire trust and cooperation in others.
Why do we dream at all?
Dreams arise because the brain remains partly active during sleep, weaving fragments of memory and sensation into images.
What causes nightmares?
Nightmares often follow a heavy meal, nervous strain, or fever, which disturb the mind's rest.
Why do children need more sleep than grown men?
Children need more sleep because their growing bodies and nervous systems require greater rest to develop properly.
Why do we sometimes talk in our sleep?
Sleep-talking happens when the mind remains partly active and speech centers stir without full waking control.
What makes a person walk in their sleep?
Sleepwalking is a disorder of the nervous system in which the body moves while the mind remains largely asleep.
Why do we forget most of our dreams?
Dreams fade quickly because the impressions they leave are faint and are not fixed firmly in memory before waking distracts the mind.
Does the full moon disturb a person's sleep?
No, careful observation shows the moon's phase has no real bearing on how well a person sleeps.
Why do people snore?
Snoring occurs when the passage of breath through the nose or throat is partly obstructed during sleep.
Why do we yawn before going to bed?
A yawn before bed is a sign of fatigue, drawing in a deeper breath as the body prepares to rest.
Is it true that yawning is contagious?
Yawning does seem to spread among people nearby, though the exact reason for this sympathy is not yet fully explained.
Why do our eyes sometimes move while we sleep?
The eyes move during certain periods of sleep because the mind is dreaming vividly and the eye muscles respond to that activity.
What causes the feeling of being unable to move when waking suddenly?
This brief paralysis occurs in a transitional state between sleep and waking, when the body has not yet caught up with the mind.
Why does a heavy supper give a person strange dreams?
A heavy supper burdens the digestion, and this discomfort disturbs sleep, producing more vivid or troubled dreams.
Why do old people often sleep less than the young?
As people age, their nervous systems generally require less deep rest, so older persons often sleep fewer hours.
Can a dream truly foretell the future?
Dreams reflect our own thoughts, fears, and memories, and have no genuine power to foretell coming events.
Why do we sometimes wake with a start, feeling we are falling?
This sudden jolt is a harmless twitch of the muscles as the body relaxes deeply on the edge of sleep.
Why does counting sheep help a restless mind fall asleep?
Counting gives the restless mind a simple, repetitive task that eases it away from troubling thoughts toward sleep.
Why do dreams often seem to occur in a strange, disordered order?
Dreams appear disordered because the sleeping mind loosely combines memories and impressions without the logic of waking thought.
Why does warm milk before bed help one sleep?
Warm milk is soothing and mildly comforting, and the ritual of a warm drink helps relax the body before sleep.
Why do some people remember their dreams vividly while others recall almost nothing?
How clearly a person remembers dreams depends chiefly on how soon after waking the mind attends to them before they fade.
Why does bread rise when left with yeast?
Yeast is a living organism that ferments the sugars in dough, releasing carbon dioxide gas whose bubbles cause the bread to rise.
What causes indigestion after a heavy meal?
Indigestion after a heavy meal generally results from the stomach's muscles and gastric juices being overtaxed by too great a quantity of food at once.
Why does milk turn sour if left out?
Milk sours because bacteria naturally present in it multiply and convert its sugar into lactic acid, curdling the proteins.
How does the body get energy from the food we eat?
Digestion breaks food down into simpler substances such as sugars and fats, which the blood carries to the tissues to be used or stored as energy.
Why do some foods spoil faster than others?
Moist, nutrient-rich foods spoil faster because they provide ideal conditions for the growth of bacteria and moulds already present on them.
What makes an apple turn brown after it is sliced?
The apple browns because enzymes in its flesh react with oxygen in the air, producing brown pigments where the surface is exposed.
Why do we feel hungry?
Hunger arises when the stomach is empty and blood sugar falls, prompting nerve signals that create the sensation of appetite.
How does chewing help with digestion?
Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces and mixes it with saliva, which begins the breakdown of starches and eases the stomach's later task.
Why does cheese develop mould if kept too long?
Cheese develops mould because microscopic fungal spores in the air settle on it and grow, feeding on its moisture and nutrients.
What gives lemons their sour taste?
Lemons taste sour because they contain a high concentration of citric acid, which stimulates the tongue's sour-sensing nerves.
Why does drinking very cold water sometimes upset the stomach?
Very cold water can temporarily slow stomach muscle activity and reduce digestive efficiency until the water warms to body temperature.
How does the body digest fatty foods?
Fat digestion relies chiefly on bile from the liver, which breaks fat into tiny droplets that digestive enzymes can then act upon.
Why does bread go stale?
Bread goes stale because its starch molecules gradually rearrange and lose moisture, making the crumb firmer and drier.
What causes the stomach to make rumbling noises?
Stomach rumbling is caused by muscular contractions moving air, fluid, and food through the digestive tract, especially when it is partly empty.
Why do onions make our eyes water when cut?
Cutting an onion releases a volatile sulphur compound that reacts with moisture in the eye to form a mild irritant, provoking tears.
How does salt help preserve meat?
Salt preserves meat by drawing out moisture through osmosis, creating an environment in which spoilage bacteria cannot easily multiply.
Why does fruit ferment if left too long?
Fruit ferments because wild yeasts naturally present on its skin consume the sugars and convert them into alcohol and carbon dioxide.
What causes the sensation of thirst?
Thirst arises when the body senses reduced water content in the blood, prompting the brain to signal a need to drink.
Why does boiling an egg make the white turn solid?
Boiling causes the proteins in the egg white to unfold and bond together, a process called denaturation, which turns the liquid solid.
How does the body get rid of food it cannot use?
Undigested matter passes through the intestines and is expelled from the body as waste, after the useful nutrients have been absorbed.
Why can birds fly through the air while most other creatures cannot?
Birds fly owing to light hollow bones, powerful breast muscles, and feathers shaped to produce lift and thrust.
How do birds manage to stay aloft for hours without growing weary?
Soaring birds ride rising currents of warm air, gliding upon them so as to spare their muscles from constant effort.
Why do wild geese fly in that neat V-shaped formation?
Flying in a V lessens the resistance each bird meets, for those behind ride the wake left by the leader.
How do birds know the proper season to begin their migration?
Shortening days, falling temperatures, and dwindling food supply signal the season and rouse the bird's instinct to depart.
Why do birds not freeze when flying at great heights where the air is cold?
Dense plumage traps warmth close to the body, while a swift metabolism keeps the bird's blood hot even in cold air.
Why do certain birds choose to fly by night rather than day?
Flying by night lets migrating birds avoid the heat and many daytime predators, steering by the stars instead.
How does a hummingbird manage to hover in one place in the air?
The hummingbird's wings sweep in a rapid figure-eight, producing lift on both the forward and backward stroke.
Why do birds' bones seem so light and hollow?
The bones are hollow yet braced with fine internal struts, giving lightness for flight without loss of strength.
How do birds find their way over thousands of miles of migration?
Birds steer by the sun and stars, sense the earth's magnetic field, and mark familiar landmarks along their route.
Why does an owl fly so silently through the night?
Soft, fringed edges upon the owl's feathers break up the turbulence of its wingbeat, muffling all sound.
Why do some birds sing even while in flight?
Song sung aloft proclaims territory or calls to a mate, and costs the bird little in the effort of flying.
How fast is a bird able to fly?
Most small birds fly some twenty to thirty miles an hour, though a diving falcon may exceed two hundred.
Why do birds often circle about before finally coming down to land?
Circling lets a bird judge the wind's direction and slow itself gradually before it settles to the ground.
Why do birds so often travel together in flocks?
Flocking together affords protection from predators and helps the birds discover feeding grounds more readily.
How do birds keep their sight so keen while flying at such speed?
A bird's eye has a swift-acting membrane and rapid vision that together keep its sight clear even in fast flight.
Why does a sleeping bird not tumble from its perch in the night?
A bird's tendons draw its toes shut about the perch automatically once the leg bends, needing no waking effort.
Why do vultures wheel about so high in the sky for hours at a time?
Vultures ride the rising warm air to spare their strength while scanning the ground below for carrion.
How can birds breathe well enough to fly where the air grows thin?
Birds possess air sacs and a one-way flow of breath through the lungs that draw far more oxygen from thin air than ours can.
Why must a young bird be taught before it can truly fly?
A fledgling's wing muscles must strengthen with practice, and instinct is sharpened by watching the example of its elders.
Why can some birds glide a long way through the air without flapping their wings at all?
A gliding bird makes use of rising air currents and the shape of its wings to stay aloft while expending little effort.
Why do maggots appear in meat left out in the summer?
Flies lay their eggs upon the meat, and these eggs hatch into maggots within a day or two.
How does a firefly produce its glow?
The firefly's glow comes from a chemical reaction called bioluminescence occurring in special organs in its abdomen.
Why do bees dance about after visiting flowers?
The dance is a means of communicating to other bees the direction and distance of the food source they have found.
What causes a person to itch after a mosquito bite?
The mosquito injects saliva that the body's immune system reacts to, producing itching and swelling.
Why do moths fly toward candle flames at night?
Moths mistake the flame for the moon or stars, which they normally use to steer a straight course, and so are confused by the nearer light.
How do ants find their way back to the nest after foraging?
Ants lay down a trail of scent as they walk, which they and their fellows follow back to the nest.
Why do crickets chirp mostly at night?
Crickets chirp by rubbing their wings together, and they are most active at night when predators are fewer and the air is calmer for carrying sound.
What makes a bee sting painful?
The sting injects a venom containing proteins that irritate nerve endings and cause inflammation.
Why do locusts sometimes appear in enormous swarms?
Under crowded conditions certain grasshoppers change form and behavior, becoming migratory locusts that gather into vast swarms.
How does a caterpillar become a butterfly?
Within the pupa the caterpillar's tissues are reorganized into the adult butterfly's body through a process called metamorphosis.
Why do flies seem to appear so quickly around rotting fruit?
Flies are attracted by the odour of fermentation and lay eggs upon the fruit, which hatch swiftly into larvae.
What causes the buzzing sound a bee makes in flight?
The buzzing sound is produced by the rapid vibration of the bee's wings as it beats them in flight.
Why do some beetles play dead when disturbed?
Playing dead, or feigning death, is a defensive instinct that makes the beetle less appealing to predators seeking live prey.
How do spiders spin their webs?
Spiders produce silk from special glands and spin it into webs using their spinnerets, guided by instinct.
Why do ants seem to carry loads far heavier than themselves?
An ant's strength relative to its size is great because muscle strength scales differently than body weight as size decreases.
What makes ladybird beetles red with black spots?
The red and black coloring comes from pigments in the beetle's exoskeleton and serves as a warning to predators of its bitter taste.
Why do dragonflies hover so precisely over water?
Dragonflies control their four wings independently, allowing them fine mastery of hovering flight near water where they hunt and breed.
How do termites manage to destroy wooden beams so thoroughly?
Termites feed upon the cellulose in wood, digesting it with the aid of microorganisms living in their gut.
Why do certain insects glow blue-green rather than yellow?
The colour of an insect's bioluminescence depends on the particular chemical composition of the light-producing reaction in its body.
What causes a swarm of gnats to gather in a cloud on a still evening?
Male gnats gather in swarms at dusk as part of their mating behavior, often near a landmark such as a person or tree.
Is the earth truly round, or is it flat as it appears when I look out across the fields?
The earth is a sphere, very slightly flattened at the poles, as proven by circumnavigation and the curve one observes at sea.
If the earth is round, why do the people on the far side not simply fall off into the sky?
Gravity draws every object toward the earth's centre, so 'down' always means toward that centre, whichever side one stands upon.
What is it that keeps our great earth suspended in the heavens without falling?
The earth is not resting upon anything; it moves freely through space, held in its path about the sun by the sun's gravitational pull.
Why do we have day followed by night, over and over?
The earth spins upon its own axis once each day, turning each region alternately toward and away from the sun's light.
Why does summer give way to winter and then to summer again?
The seasons result from the tilt of the earth's axis, which causes each hemisphere to lean toward or away from the sun through the year.
What is the true cause of an earthquake?
Earthquakes arise when strain built up between great plates of the earth's crust is suddenly released along a fault.
What causes a mountain to spew forth fire and smoke, as Vesuvius does?
A volcano is fed by molten rock, called magma, forced upward through the crust by great heat and pressure from within the earth.
Why does the sea rise and fall upon the shore twice each day?
The tides are caused chiefly by the moon's gravitational pull upon the waters of the earth, with the sun's pull adding a lesser effect.
Why does a compass needle always point toward the north?
The needle aligns with the earth's own magnetic field, which behaves much as though a great magnet lay within the planet, roughly along its axis.
What lies at the very centre of the earth, deep beneath our feet?
At the earth's centre lies a dense core, believed to be chiefly iron and nickel, exceedingly hot and under immense pressure.
How do great mountain ranges such as the Alps come to be formed?
Mountains are raised slowly over vast ages as the earth's crust folds and buckles under the pressure of colliding land masses.
Why does a ship sailing out to sea seem to sink from view, hull first, before the masts?
The ship disappears hull first because the surface of the sea curves away beneath it, proof that the earth's surface is round.
How large a body is the earth, that ships may sail so long without reaching its end?
The earth measures very nearly twenty-five thousand miles about its equator, a figure established by careful survey and calculation.
Why is it bitterly cold near the poles and warm near the equator?
The sun's rays strike the equator most directly and the poles most obliquely, owing to the curve of the earth, so heat is spread unevenly.
Why do all rivers run down toward the sea and never away from it?
Rivers flow toward the sea because gravity draws water downhill, from higher ground toward the lower level of the ocean.
Why is there so much ice gathered always at the poles of the earth?
The poles are cold chiefly because sunlight strikes them at so oblique an angle that little of its warmth is absorbed there.
How did the dry land and the wide oceans come to be divided as they are upon the earth?
The present arrangement of continents and oceans has developed over vast ages through the slow shifting and separation of great crustal plates.
Why does the North Star seem to stand still while all the other stars wheel about it?
The North Star lies almost exactly above the earth's axis of rotation, so as the earth spins the other stars appear to circle about it.
Why does everything upon the earth fall downward rather than float off into the sky?
Every object is drawn downward by the earth's gravity, a force of attraction that every body of matter exerts upon every other.
Is it true that a ship sailing too far out upon the ocean might reach the edge of the world and fall away?
There is no edge to fall from, for the earth is round and a ship sailing on in one direction will simply return, in time, to its starting point.
Why does a rainbow show so many colours?
A rainbow appears because sunlight is refracted and reflected within countless raindrops, which split white light into its component colours according to wavelength.
What is white light actually made of?
White light is a mixture of all the colours of the spectrum, which can be separated by a prism and recombined to appear white again.
Why is the sky blue?
The sky is blue because the atmosphere scatters the shorter, blue wavelengths of sunlight more strongly than the longer, red ones.
Why does the sun turn red at sunset?
At sunset, sunlight passes through more atmosphere, which scatters away the blue light and leaves the longer red and orange wavelengths to reach our eyes.
How many colours are there truly in the rainbow?
The rainbow's spectrum is a continuous gradation of wavelengths; the seven named bands are a traditional convenience rather than a strict natural division.
Why do soap bubbles show swirling colours?
Soap bubbles show colours because light reflecting off the front and back of the thin film interferes, reinforcing some wavelengths and cancelling others.
Why does a prism split light into colours?
A prism splits light because glass bends different wavelengths by different amounts, spreading white light into its constituent colours.
Why do leaves turn yellow and red in autumn?
In autumn, chlorophyll breaks down and its green fades, revealing yellow and orange pigments already present, while some leaves also form new red pigments.
Why is grass green?
Grass is green because its cells contain chlorophyll, a pigment that absorbs red and blue light while reflecting green.
Why does the sea appear blue?
The sea appears blue chiefly because water absorbs red light more than blue, and blue light is scattered back to the eye.
Can two rainbows appear together in the sky?
Yes, a secondary rainbow can form from light reflecting twice inside raindrops, appearing fainter and with its colours reversed.
Why does a peacock's feather shimmer with colour?
The peacock's feather shimmers because microscopic ridges on its surface scatter light through interference, producing colour without any pigment.
Why do we see a halo of colour around the moon sometimes?
A coloured ring about the moon is caused by moonlight refracting through ice crystals or water droplets high in the atmosphere.
Why does mixing blue and yellow paint make green?
Mixing blue and yellow pigments makes green because each absorbs different wavelengths, and the light left unabsorbed by both appears green.
Why does a stained-glass window glow with colour when the sun shines through it?
Stained glass glows with colour because metallic oxides mixed into the glass absorb certain wavelengths of light and transmit others.
Why does the northern lights display so many colours?
The northern lights show colour because charged particles from the sun strike gases in the upper atmosphere, and each gas glows a characteristic hue when excited.
Why do some flowers appear more vivid in colour than others?
Flowers appear more vivid when they contain a greater concentration of pigments, such as anthocyanins or carotenoids, in their petal cells.
Why does ice sometimes look blue rather than clear?
Thick ice looks blue because it absorbs red light over longer distances, allowing more blue light to be transmitted or reflected.
Why does the colour of a candle flame change near its base and its tip?
The flame changes colour because temperature and the completeness of combustion vary through the flame, producing blue where burning is hottest and yellow where soot glows.
Why does light through red glass make everything look red?
Red glass allows mainly red wavelengths to pass through while absorbing the others, so anything seen through it appears tinted red.
What makes a steam engine's piston move back and forth inside its cylinder?
The piston is driven by the pressure of expanding steam admitted alternately to each side of the cylinder, pushing it first one way and then the other.
Why must the joints and bearings of an engine be kept well oiled?
Oil forms a thin film between moving surfaces that greatly reduces friction, preventing needless wear and the generation of excess heat.
Why does a heavy flywheel help an engine run so smoothly?
A flywheel stores momentum by virtue of its mass and rotation, releasing it steadily to smooth out the irregular pushes delivered by the pistons.
What causes an old, neglected boiler to explode?
Explosion occurs when steam pressure rises beyond what the boiler's plates and safety valve can bear, commonly through low water or a stuck valve.
How does the pendulum of a clock keep such regular time?
The pendulum's period depends chiefly upon its length and the pull of gravity, which together keep its swing very nearly constant.
How is a heavy elevator car raised with so little apparent strain on the motor?
A motor winds the cable about a drum while a counterweight on the opposite side balances much of the load, so far less force is required.
How does a dynamo produce electricity out of mere spinning motion?
A dynamo generates electricity because a coil of wire turning within a magnetic field induces a flow of current, as Faraday first showed.
Why do gears of different sizes turning together change a machine's speed?
Gears of different sizes change speed because the smaller must revolve more times than the larger to keep their meshing teeth in step, altering the ratio of turning.
Why does iron machinery left out of doors soon grow rusty?
Rust forms when iron reacts chemically with oxygen and moisture in the air, the surface gradually turning to iron oxide.
How does a modern refrigerator keep food cold without any ice at all?
A special gas is compressed and then allowed to expand and evaporate inside the box, absorbing heat there and releasing it outside.
How does a pump manage to draw water up from deep in a well?
A pump creates a partial vacuum above the water, allowing the greater pressure of the outside air to push it up through the pipe.
Why does a motor car's engine grow so very hot after a long journey?
Heat is produced by the friction of moving parts and the burning of fuel, and it accumulates faster than the cooling system can carry it away.
What makes a turbine wheel spin so swiftly under a jet of steam?
The turbine spins because the moving steam strikes its curved blades and transfers its momentum, driving the wheel around.
Why does a bicycle stay upright while rolling, though it falls at once when still?
A moving bicycle stays upright because its spinning wheels resist changes to their axis, and the rider's small steering corrections keep it balanced.
What causes an engine to knock or rattle sharply when under heavy strain?
Knocking occurs when the fuel and air mixture ignites unevenly or too soon in the cylinder, producing a sharp secondary explosion instead of a smooth burn.
How does a battery manage to store electricity for later use?
A battery stores energy through a chemical reaction between its plates and the acid within, a reaction that can be reversed to yield a current.
How does a ship's propeller manage to push so great a vessel through the water?
The propeller's angled blades act much as a screw does, driving water backward and so pushing the ship forward by reaction.
What is the purpose of the governor fitted atop many steam engines?
The governor's weights fly outward as speed increases, automatically closing the throttle so that the engine's speed is kept steady.
Why does a motor car sometimes backfire with a startling report?
Backfire happens when unburned fuel ignites within the exhaust pipe or intake, usually because of a mistimed spark or valve.
How does a windmill turn the ordinary motion of the air into useful work?
The wind, pressing against the angled sails, turns the shaft, and this rotary motion is carried down to drive the millstones or other machinery.
Why do we have four seasons each year?
The seasons arise because the earth's axis is tilted as it orbits the sun, so different regions receive more or less direct sunlight through the year.
Why are the days longer in summer than in winter?
Because the earth is tilted on its axis, the northern hemisphere leans toward the sun in summer, giving it more hours of daylight than in winter.
Why does autumn feel cooler than summer even though the sun still shines?
Autumn feels cooler because the sun's angle grows lower and days shorter, so less of its energy reaches and warms the ground.
Why do leaves change colour and fall in the autumn?
Leaves change colour because shortening days and cooler weather cause the green chlorophyll to break down, revealing other pigments before the leaf falls.
Why is it that a year has twelve months?
There are twelve months because the calendar was arranged to approximate twelve cycles of the moon occurring within one solar year.
Why does a day last twenty-four hours?
A day lasts about twenty-four hours because that is the time the earth takes to complete one full rotation upon its own axis.
Why is winter the coldest season of the year?
Winter is coldest because the hemisphere is tilted away from the sun, receiving weaker and more slanting sunlight for a shorter part of each day.
Why do the stars seem to shift position with the seasons?
The stars appear to shift because the earth's yearly orbit around the sun changes our position, so different constellations become visible at different times of year.
Why does it take a full year for the seasons to repeat?
The seasons repeat yearly because that is the time the earth requires to complete one full orbit around the sun.
Why do we add an extra day in leap years?
The extra day is added because the earth's orbit takes about 365 and a quarter days, so every four years the calendar must gain a day to stay accurate.
Why does the sun rise earlier in summer than in winter?
The sun rises earlier in summer because the earth's tilt brings that hemisphere closer to constant sunlight, shortening the night.
Why is spring the season when plants begin to grow again?
Plants grow again in spring because rising temperatures and lengthening daylight provide the warmth and light needed for growth to resume.
Why do the hours of daylight change gradually rather than all at once?
Daylight changes gradually because the earth's tilt shifts its exposure to the sun little by little each day as it moves along its orbit.
Why does the moon appear full only once a month?
The moon appears full once a month because that is how long it takes to orbit the earth and be fully lit by the sun as seen from here.
Why is midsummer's day the longest day of the year?
Midsummer's day is longest because it marks the point when that hemisphere is tilted most directly toward the sun, giving the greatest hours of daylight.
Why does the shortest day of the year fall in winter?
The shortest day falls in winter because the hemisphere is then tilted farthest from the sun, giving the least hours of daylight in the year.
Why do some years have an extra week of winter weather while others do not?
Winters vary because shifting patterns of wind and ocean currents change from year to year, altering how long cold weather persists.
Why does the sun appear to move across the sky differently in each season?
The sun's apparent path shifts because the earth's tilted axis changes the angle at which we view the sun as it circles through the year.
Why does time seem to pass at the same steady rate every day?
Time passes at a steady rate because the earth's rotation and orbit occur with remarkable regularity, giving us a reliable measure of hours and days.
Why are the peoples who live near the equator dark of skin?
Their skin is rich in a pigment called melanin, which over many generations has served to shield the skin from the sun's strong rays; children of other stock do not darken merely by living there.
Why do the peoples of the far north build their houses of snow?
Snow, being full of trapped air, is a poor conductor of heat and so insulates the hut against the fierce outer cold, while a small lamp within warms the enclosed air.
Why do travelers say the air of the tropics breeds fever?
Tropical fevers such as malaria are carried by the bite of certain mosquitoes that thrive in warm, wet climates, and not by the air itself.
Why are the peoples of high mountain lands said to be short of breath when first there?
The air at great heights is thinner and holds less oxygen, so the newcomer's blood cannot draw sufficient breath until his body slowly adjusts.
Why do desert peoples wear such heavy robes despite the great heat?
Loose, heavy robes actually shield the skin from the sun's direct rays and slow the loss of the body's moisture, keeping the wearer cooler than bare skin would.
Why do the peoples of the Orient bow rather than shake hands in greeting?
Bowing is simply a long-established custom of courtesy in China, Japan, and neighboring lands, no more mysterious than our own handshake, its depth varying with the respect intended.
Why do the old accounts call the deep forests of Africa the cradle of mankind?
Fossil remains recovered in Africa suggest that the earliest ancestors of man arose there, spreading afterward to other continents over a vast stretch of time.
Why do the people of Japan live upon a chain of islands rather than a mainland?
Japan's islands were shaped by volcanic and geological upheaval along the rim of the Pacific, and its people settled them by sea from the Asian mainland in ancient times.
Why do the peoples of Arctic lands see the sun at midnight in summer?
Because the earth is tilted upon its axis, the polar regions face the sun continuously for part of the year, giving the far north its famous midnight sun in summer.
Why do certain river tribes of South America build their houses upon stilts?
Stilts raise the floor above the river's seasonal floods, keeping the dwelling dry and cool and safer from crawling creatures below.
Why do the Chinese eat with chopsticks rather than fork and knife?
Chopsticks developed as a practical utensil for food already cut into small pieces before cooking, a long-standing custom of Chinese cuisine.
Why do the people of India hold the cow to be sacred?
The cow's sanctity in Hindu belief rests on ancient religious tradition, the animal being valued also for its milk and its labor in the fields, so its slaughter is generally forbidden.
Why do the Bedouin of the desert travel by camel rather than by horse?
The camel can go many days without water and thrives on the sparse desert plants, making it far better suited than the horse to long desert journeys.
Why are the peoples of the high Andes said to be short in stature?
Their compact build and larger lung capacity are inherited traits, favored over many generations, well suited to breathing the thin air of high altitude.
How do the islanders of Polynesia find their way across such open ocean?
Skilled Polynesian navigators read the stars, ocean swells, cloud patterns, and the flight of birds to steer their canoes accurately across vast stretches of open sea.
Why do the Inuit of the far north eat mostly meat and fish?
The Arctic climate permits little farming, so the Inuit rely chiefly on seal, fish, and caribou, which also supply the fat needed to keep warm.
Why do the peoples of Egypt build their villages and cities along the Nile?
The Nile's annual flood deposits rich silt along its banks, making the narrow strip beside the river the only fertile ground amid the surrounding desert.
Is it true, as the old story goes, that there are no snakes in Ireland?
Ireland has no native snakes chiefly because it was cut off from the European mainland by rising seas after the last ice age, before snakes had spread that far north.
Why do the peoples of Siberia keep such great herds of reindeer?
Reindeer thrive on the lichen and moss of the tundra where crops cannot grow, providing the Siberian herding peoples with meat, milk, hide, and transport.
Why do sailors say that some remote island peoples had never before seen iron before the first ships arrived?
Such islands are often far from any source of metal ore and were settled long ago by peoples using stone, wood, and shell, before regular contact with metal-working traders.
Doctor, what is the purpose of the spleen?
The spleen filters and stores blood, removing worn-out red corpuscles and assisting the body's defense against infection.
Why do we have two kidneys instead of one?
The paired kidneys filter waste from the blood and regulate water and salts, and having two provides a safeguard should one be injured.
What causes the heart to beat?
The heart beats because of electrical impulses generated in its own tissue, which cause the heart muscle to contract rhythmically.
What is the function of the liver?
The liver processes nutrients from digestion, filters toxins from the blood, and produces bile to aid in digesting fats.
Why do our fingernails grow?
Fingernails grow continuously because living cells at their root divide and push older, hardened cells outward.
What causes a fever when one is ill?
A fever arises when the body raises its internal temperature to fight infection, aided by chemical signals from the immune system.
What is the purpose of the appendix?
The appendix is now understood to harbor beneficial bacteria and to play a small role in the body's immune defenses.
Why does the stomach growl when we are hungry?
The growling comes from muscular contractions moving air and fluid through an empty stomach and intestines.
What causes our hair to turn grey with age?
Grey hair results from the gradual loss of pigment-producing cells at the hair follicle as a person ages.
Why do we have a gallbladder?
The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver, releasing it to help digest fats in the small intestine.
What is the function of the lungs?
The lungs take in oxygen from the air and pass it into the blood, while removing carbon dioxide from the body.
Why do our eyes water when we cry?
Tears are produced by glands above the eyes and are released in greater quantity under emotional strain as a reflex response.
What causes goosebumps when we are cold?
Goosebumps occur when tiny muscles at the base of each hair follicle contract, raising the hair to conserve warmth.
Why does one part of the brain seem to control thought and another feeling?
Different regions of the brain specialize in particular functions, such as reasoning, memory, and emotion, though they act together as a whole.
What is the purpose of the pancreas?
The pancreas produces digestive enzymes and also secretes insulin, which regulates the amount of sugar in the blood.
Why do we sweat when we exert ourselves?
Sweating helps cool the body by evaporation, released by glands in the skin as muscular activity raises internal heat.
What causes the pulse we feel at the wrist?
The pulse is the rhythmic expansion of an artery caused by blood being pumped through it with each heartbeat.
Why does a broken bone heal itself over time?
A broken bone heals as the body forms new bone tissue, with cells called osteoblasts gradually bridging and hardening the fracture.
What is the role of the bladder?
The bladder stores urine produced by the kidneys until it is convenient for the body to release it.
Why do we yawn when we are tired?
Yawning is thought to help increase alertness by drawing in more air and stretching the muscles of the jaw and face.
