Why does it thunder after a flash of lightning?
Thunder is the sound produced when lightning heats the air so suddenly that it expands and rushes outward, creating a shock wave we hear as a crack or rumble.
Why do we see our breath on a cold morning?
Warm, moist air from the lungs meets the cold outside air and the water vapour condenses into tiny droplets, forming a visible cloud.
What makes hail form during a summer storm?
Hail forms when strong updrafts carry raindrops repeatedly through freezing layers of a thundercloud, adding layers of ice until the stones grow heavy enough to fall.
Why does the sky turn greenish before a severe storm?
A greenish tint often appears when late-day sunlight, reddened by its low angle, passes through a thick, hail-laden storm cloud, mixing with the cloud's natural blue-grey colour.
What causes a rainbow to appear after rain?
A rainbow appears when sunlight is refracted and reflected inside countless raindrops, splitting the light into its component colours.
Why do storms seem worse at sea than on land?
At sea, winds meet no hills or forests to slow them, so they blow harder and raise larger waves than they would over land.
What causes fog to settle over a valley at night?
Fog forms when moist air near the ground cools below its dew point overnight, causing the water vapour to condense into tiny droplets suspended in the air.
Why does lightning strike tall trees and towers more often?
Lightning tends to strike the tallest or most conductive objects because they offer the shortest path for the electrical charge between cloud and ground.
Why is snow white instead of clear like ice?
Snow appears white because its many tiny ice crystals scatter all wavelengths of visible light equally, rather than transmitting light straight through as clear ice does.
What causes a tornado to form during a thunderstorm?
A tornado forms when a rotating updraft within a severe thunderstorm tightens and stretches, drawing air inward and downward to spin at great speed near the ground.
Why does distant thunder sound like a low rumble rather than a sharp crack?
As sound travels far, its higher frequencies fade more quickly than the lower ones, and echoes from the long lightning channel blend together into a rumble.
What causes dew to form on the grass in the early morning?
Dew forms when the ground and grass cool overnight, chilling the air just above them until moisture condenses out as tiny droplets.
Why do storm clouds appear dark grey or black?
Storm clouds look dark because they are thick with water droplets and ice, which block much of the sunlight from passing through to the ground below.
What makes a hurricane spin in a circular pattern?
A hurricane spins due to the Earth's rotation, which deflects the inflowing winds around the storm's low-pressure centre, a effect known as the Coriolis force.
Why does a barometer fall before a storm arrives?
A barometer falls before a storm because the approaching low-pressure system reduces the weight of the air pressing down upon the mercury column.
What causes a whirlwind to pick up dust on a dry day?
A dust whirlwind forms when hot air rises quickly from a heated patch of ground, and the surrounding air rushes in to replace it, creating a spinning column.
Why does rain fall in drops instead of a continuous sheet?
Falling water breaks into drops because surface tension pulls the water into small rounded shapes as it separates from the cloud and descends through the air.
What causes the loud cracking sound sometimes heard when lightning strikes very close by?
A close strike produces a sharp crack because the lightning channel is so near that the shock wave from its rapid heating of the air reaches the ear almost instantly and undiminished.
Why do the stars seem to twinkle in the night sky?
Starlight twinkles because it passes through moving layers of our own atmosphere, of differing temperature and density, which bend the light this way and that.
What makes the Moon change shape from night to night?
The Moon's phases come from the changing angle at which sunlight falls upon it as it circles the Earth, showing us more or less of its lit half.
Why does the planet Mars glow red in the sky?
Mars appears red because its rocks and soil are rich in iron oxide, the same rust-colored substance found in old iron left out in the rain.
What are the streaks of light people call shooting stars?
Shooting stars are small fragments of rock and dust that burn brightly as they plunge into our atmosphere at great speed.
Why does the sky turn dark at night?
The sky darkens at night because the Earth turns upon its axis, carrying our side away from the Sun's light.
What exactly is the pale band of light called the Milky Way?
The Milky Way is the combined glow of countless millions of distant stars in our own galaxy, seen edge-on from within it.
Why does the Sun rise in the east and set in the west?
The Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west because the Earth spins from west to east upon its axis.
What brings about a lunar eclipse?
A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, so that the Earth's shadow falls upon the Moon's face.
What are the bright rings that circle the planet Saturn?
Saturn's rings are made up of countless small particles of ice and rock, circling the planet in a broad, flat band.
Why do we have day and night at all?
Day and night occur because the Earth rotates on its own axis once roughly every twenty-four hours, turning each part toward and away from the Sun.
What causes the changing seasons through the year?
The seasons change because the Earth's axis is tilted, so different parts of the globe receive more or less direct sunlight as the Earth journeys around the Sun.
Why do comets grow those long glowing tails?
A comet's tail forms when the Sun's heat and light drive off gas and dust from the comet's icy body as it nears the Sun.
Why do the planets shine steadily while the stars twinkle so?
Planets shine steadily because they appear as tiny discs rather than mere points, so the shimmer of our atmosphere averages out across their breadth.
Why does the North Star never seem to move in the sky?
The North Star lies almost directly above the Earth's axis of rotation, so as the Earth turns, that one point in the sky appears to stay still.
How far away are the stars we see twinkling at night?
The stars lie at enormous distances, so far that their light, though traveling at tremendous speed, takes years or even centuries to reach us.
What keeps the planets moving around the Sun instead of flying off into space?
The planets are held in their orbits by the Sun's gravity, which pulls them inward even as their own motion carries them forward.
What is the Sun actually made of?
The Sun is a vast ball of exceedingly hot gas, chiefly hydrogen, which generates its light and heat from processes deep within its core.
Why does the Moon look so much larger when it is near the horizon?
The Moon only seems larger near the horizon; it is an illusion of our eye and mind, for its actual size and distance scarcely change.
What causes the dark spots sometimes seen upon the Sun's face?
Sunspots are regions of intense magnetic activity on the Sun's surface that are slightly cooler than their surroundings, making them appear dark by contrast.
Why do bears sleep through the winter?

Bears retire to dens and pass into a deep winter sleep because food grows scarce and their bodily processes slow to conserve stored fat. They rouse again as the weather warms and food becomes plentiful.
Why do birds fly south in the autumn?

Birds migrate south each autumn to follow warmer climates and abundant food, returning north again in spring to breed. This seasonal journey is guided by instinct, daylight length, and inherited habit.
Why does a cat purr?
A cat purrs through the rhythmic action of its laryngeal muscles and diaphragm, most often when it is relaxed, contented, or seeking comfort. Kittens also purr while nursing.
Why do dogs bark at strangers?
Dogs bark at strangers chiefly to warn their pack or household of an unfamiliar presence, a trait inherited from their wild ancestors who lived and hunted in groups.
Why do moths fly toward a lamp at night?
Moths are drawn to artificial light because it disrupts their natural navigation by the moon and stars, causing them to circle the nearer, brighter source in confusion.
Why does a chameleon change its colour?

A chameleon changes colour through special cells in its skin that expand or contract, altering its hue in response to temperature, light, and its own emotional state, often to blend with surroundings.
Why do salmon swim upstream to the place of their birth?
Salmon return to their native streams to spawn, guided by a keen sense of smell that recalls the particular waters where they hatched years before.
Why do owls see so well in darkness?
Owls see well in darkness because their large eyes contain many light-sensitive rod cells and gather what dim light exists, allowing them to hunt effectively at night.
Why does a snake shed its skin?
A snake sheds its skin because its outer layer does not grow as the animal does; the old skin is periodically cast off to make room for new growth beneath.
Why do spiders spin webs?
Spiders spin webs of silk produced by glands in their abdomen, constructing them to trap insects for food and, in some cases, to shelter their eggs.
Why do crickets chirp on summer evenings?
Male crickets chirp by rubbing specialized structures on their wings together, chiefly to attract mates and warn off rival males, most actively in warm evening weather.
Why do cuckoos lay their eggs in other birds' nests?
The cuckoo lays its eggs in the nests of other bird species as an inherited strategy, allowing the host bird to raise its young while the cuckoo is freed from that labour.
Why do bats fly about only after dark?
Bats are active mainly after dark to avoid daytime predators and to hunt insects that are themselves most numerous at night, finding their way by a remarkable sense of echo and hearing.
Why do elephants have such long trunks?
The elephant's trunk is an elongated, muscular nose and upper lip combined, used for breathing, smelling, drinking, and grasping food, having developed to suit the animal's great size and needs.
Why do fish swim together in great schools?
Fish swim in schools chiefly for protection from predators and to improve their chances of finding food, moving together through coordinated response to their neighbours' movements.
Why does the swallow return to the same barn each spring?
Swallows return each spring to familiar nesting sites because of a strong homing instinct and memory, seeking places that have proven safe and suitable for raising their young.
Why do bees form great swarms and leave the hive?
A hive swarms when it becomes overcrowded or the old queen prepares to leave; a portion of the colony departs with her to found a new nest elsewhere.
Why does an octopus change the colour of its skin?
An octopus changes colour through special pigment cells called chromatophores in its skin, which it can expand or contract at will to blend with its surroundings or signal its mood.
Why does a rooster crow at dawn?
A rooster crows at dawn largely from an internal body clock tuned to light, and also to announce his presence and territory to other roosters at daybreak.
Why do squirrels bury nuts before winter comes?
Squirrels bury nuts in autumn as an instinctive means of storing food, later relying on memory and scent to recover their hidden caches during the lean winter months.
Why do plants bend toward the window?
Plants bend toward light because their growing tips respond to it, elongating unevenly so the stem curves toward the brighter side.
What makes a seed sprout after lying dormant all winter?
A seed sprouts when warmth and moisture activate enzymes that awaken the embryo, allowing it to draw on stored food and begin growth.
Why do the leaves of the maple turn red in autumn?
As chlorophyll breaks down in autumn, it stops masking other pigments, and sugars trapped in the leaf can also form red anthocyanin compounds.
How does a climbing vine know to wind about a pole?
A climbing vine's tip sways in circles and, upon touching a support, its cells on the touching side grow more slowly, causing it to curl around the object.
Why does a potato left in a dark cellar send out pale shoots?
Without light, the shoots cannot form green chlorophyll, so they grow pale and elongated as they stretch toward any distant light source.
What causes mushrooms to appear suddenly after rain, with no seed sown?
Mushrooms grow from fine threads called mycelium already present in the soil, which send up fruiting bodies quickly once rain provides enough moisture.
Why do flowers give off scent?
Flowers produce scent from volatile oils in their petals, which attract insects that then carry pollen from one bloom to another.
How does a tree draw water up to its highest leaves?
Water rises through narrow vessels in the trunk as leaves lose moisture through evaporation, creating a continuous pull that draws water up from the roots.
Why does clover sometimes appear where none was planted?
Clover seeds can lie dormant in soil for years, or be carried in by wind, water, birds, or grazing animals, and sprout once conditions favor them.
What is the cause of a plant's leaves wilting in the heat of the day?
In great heat, a plant loses water through its leaves faster than its roots can replace it, so the leaf cells lose firmness and droop.
Why do some trees lose their leaves in autumn while pines keep theirs?
Broad leaves would lose too much water and be damaged by frost, so deciduous trees shed them, while the pine's needles are coated and shaped to endure winter cold.
How does a bean plant know which way is up when it sprouts underground?
The sprouting bean responds to gravity, with roots growing downward and the shoot growing upward, guided by cells that sense the pull of the earth.
Why do certain plants close their leaves at nightfall?
Many plants fold their leaves at night through changes in water pressure in special cells, a rhythm tied to their internal daily clock.
What makes an orange or lemon tree bear fruit only after some years of growth?
A citrus tree must grow to full maturity, developing enough leaves and root system to support flowering and fruit production, which takes several years.
Why does ivy cling so firmly to a brick wall?
Ivy clings by means of small rootlets or adhesive pads that grip tiny irregularities in the wall's surface.
How do desert plants survive with so little rain?
Desert plants often have deep or wide-spreading roots, thick water-storing tissues, and waxy coatings that greatly reduce water loss.
Why do some trees produce more fruit in one year and less the next?
Heavy fruiting one year uses up stored nutrients and reduces flower bud formation, so the tree naturally produces less fruit the following year.
What causes a garden plant to grow spindly and weak when crowded together?
Crowded plants compete for light, water, and nutrients, and often stretch thin and weak while reaching for enough sunlight to survive.
Why does grass grow greener after a thunderstorm than after ordinary rain?
Thunderstorms convert nitrogen in the air into forms that fall to earth with the rain, providing grass with a natural dose of fertilizer.
How does a cactus manage to live without visible leaves?
A cactus performs its leaf-like functions of gathering light and exchanging air through its green, fleshy stem, which also stores water efficiently.
Why does fire feel hot to the touch?
Fire is a chemical reaction called combustion, and the energy it releases as heat is what warms the skin.
Why does the sky turn red at sunset?
Sunlight is scattered by the atmosphere, and at sunset it passes through more air, so the shorter blue rays are scattered away and the red remain.
Why does a candle flame flicker even indoors?
Rising currents of warm air, set going by the flame's own heat, disturb it and make it flicker.
Why does a bar of iron glow red when heated in a forge?
When heated sufficiently, the iron's atoms vibrate energetically enough to radiate visible light, a glow that brightens as it grows hotter.
